author: sonnet
reason: A explains how the gateway handles a request today, defines every term (Key Service, plan, window, fail open), and walks through the steps and failure cases in order, including what happens to Enterprise customers and to Key Service failures. B assumes more background and leaves the Enterprise path undefined.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the better handover for someone new to the project: it starts with how the gateway works today and defines its terms before describing the change, walks through the request in numbered steps, collects every failure case in one table, and says what happens to Enterprise customers until Product picks a limit, which A leaves undefined.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with a summary of the current system and its numbers, explains each part (writes, copy, sweeper, comparer, backfill, switch, IDs, reads) apart from the rollout order, and ends with a failure table, so an outsider can build a full picture of how the system works; B is tighter but mixes how things work into the rollout steps and gives no overview.

author: haiku
reason: B gives the system's context first (row counts, load, how ids and versions are assigned, the existing replica and job system). It then explains each mechanism in its own section, separate from the rollout steps: the write paths per mode, the copy, the sweeper, the comparer, IDs, read fallback, plus a failure table. A is tighter but spreads that explanation across the steps, so a newcomer has to rebuild the design from them.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with the load numbers, a four-phase overview and every term defined before it is used, and it keeps how the system runs (write, delete, sweeper and read flows) separate from the rollout steps, with a table of failure cases at the end, so a newcomer can build the full picture faster than from B, which spreads its explanation through an 11-step runbook and has no failure summary.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer more to orient by: the current system and its scale, a four-phase overview, a definition of how `version` is maintained (A relies on it without explaining it), a runtime walkthrough of each write, sweep and read path, a failure table and explicit open questions, so it is easier to understand how the system works before reading the steps.

author: haiku
reason: A is longer and repeats itself, but it pins down how the system behaves: a per-origin table of which rollback steps run, how billing_mode behaves during a rollback, a failure table, and clearly marked unknowns, while B reads more easily but leaves gaps (what a rollback from shadow does), adds claims the brief does not make (reconcile prevents double charges, gates read comparison_results), and draws decommission as automatic.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer, but I'd rather be handed it: it says which rollback steps run from each mode, where billing_mode stands during a rollback, that forward moves are refused while one is running, and what each failure leads to, and it marks what the brief leaves unstated, so I wouldn't have to guess at the gaps A skips.

author: sonnet
reason: A names every moving part (the rollout tool, billing monitor, rollback record, charging-paused switch, stop point and payment provider) and spells out how each gate is evaluated, what each rollback step does for each start mode, and how reconcile avoids double charges against the provider; B reads more easily, with its labeled diagram and mode table, but leaves those mechanisms vague.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains the actual mechanisms that A leaves vague: how charging is paused (a separate switch), where catch_up starts (a recorded stop point), how duplicate ledger entries are avoided, how reconcile works against the payment provider with the ledger winning, which rollback steps run from each start mode, and what is still undecided. A's labelled diagram and mode table are tidier, but B tells me more about how the system really works.

author: haiku
reason: Document B is easier to start reading, with clearer service roles and a guide to its diagram, but A is the one that shows how the system actually works: every step names its owner, its trigger, how services talk to each other and what each stores, and it handles unreachable services and broker failures, while B leaves holes such as no PaymentSucceeded event, no account of how Inventory learns a payment succeeded, and no record of a successful charge.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a plain summary and the three rules behind the design, then gives numbered steps that say what starts each step, which service does it and what each database stores, and ends with a table of failures. A is lighter to read but leaves real gaps: it never says which service coordinates the steps after payment, it has no success event or success status for a charge, and it skips what happens when a service cannot be reached.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to skim because of its service table and swimlane diagram, but A gives a complete and consistent account of how the system really works: one coordinator owns the status, idempotency by order id, the outbox, the crash sweep, timeouts and late or unmatched webhooks, all tied together by a failure table. B says Order coordinates, yet its diagram shows services triggering each other directly by events, and it says nothing about technical failures or crashes.

author: sonnet
reason: A is cleaner and its per-service swimlanes are easier to scan, but B explains how the system behaves when things go wrong: timeouts, crashes, lost or repeated events (outbox, recovery sweep, idempotent calls), late charges after Order gives up, and an honest list of open questions, so it gives a smart newcomer a more complete and trustworthy picture.

author: haiku
reason: A explains today's system first, follows one notification through the new runtime path in order, and lists failures in one table, so I could understand how the system works; B splits the runtime design across its rollout steps and leaves out key mechanics such as how leases interact with retries.

author: haiku
reason: B is the better handover for someone new to the project: it opens with how today's system works and why it has to change, lists the rules the design must keep, follows one notification from creation to send, and collects the failure cases in one table, whereas A mixes the description of the system into its deployment steps, so the reader has to piece the design together.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains why the change is needed, defines every term first, and then follows one notification end to end through the system with a single failure table, while B arranges the same mechanics by rollout step, so a newcomer has to piece together how it runs from eight separate sections.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer: it states today's problem, defines every term (outbox, row lock, handed_off, route), and walks through the runtime flow before the rollout steps, with failure modes in one scannable table, whereas A mixes how the system works into the eight shipping steps.

author: haiku
reason: Document A explains the deployment context first: two instances behind a non-sticky load balancer, which is why sessions go in Postgres. It also defines every mechanism it relies on (hashed session IDs, dummy-hash timing, atomic UPDATE, upsert), gives a reason for each choice and lists more failure cases, so an outsider can see how the system works and why; B is tighter but leaves gaps (raw session IDs as keys, a timing leak, the lock not cleared on success).

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer more of what they need to understand the system: why Postgres is used (two instances behind a load balancer with no sticky sessions), the full table schemas, the cookie flags, hashed session IDs, timing-safe handling of unknown emails, the design choices, and a fuller failure table. A is tighter but leaves the reader to guess at the schemas and the deployment context.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains why sessions live in Postgres (two instances behind a load balancer with no sticky sessions, server-rendered app). It also walks through each step with its reasoning, the transaction boundaries and what happens on each failure, so a newcomer understands how the system works and not just what it does; B is tidier but leaves out that context and those reasons.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer the context A leaves out: why state must live in Postgres (two instances, no sticky sessions), the existing users table, and which steps share one transaction. It also explains the atomic expiry check, what happens when a step fails partway, and the race it accepts. That makes it easier to understand how the system actually behaves, even though it is longer and repeats some of the diagram.

author: haiku
reason: A defines the stack terms a newcomer won't know (readiness, maxUnavailable: 0, KMS, revoke, rollback) and explains how the app reads keys before it walks through the rollout, so the runtime model is clear first; B's Starts/Does/State/If-fails layout is more uniform and covers more failure paths, but it uses terms like maxUnavailable without defining them and puts the runtime explanation after the steps that rely on it.

author: haiku
reason: B gives an outsider more to understand the system with: it explains why the keys must be rotated (git history has already leaked them), defines terms such as readiness, maxUnavailable, KMS and revoke, describes the runtime before the rollout, and says what stays in config. A is somewhat tighter operationally, but it assumes more background knowledge.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains why each piece exists, for example that clients copying the key at construction forces a redeploy. It also spells out behaviours B leaves vague: readiness stays 200 after startup even if the store goes down, each secret refreshes on its own, a stuck refresh is caught by checking each replica, and the new key is tested before it reaches the store. B is shorter and does flag the two-live-keys question, but A leaves an outsider far fewer gaps about how the system actually works.

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer, but it explains how the system works and why: why the clients currently copy keys, how the readiness probe and the rolling deploy with maxUnavailable 0 work, that /healthz stays 200 after a pod is ready, how a partial refresh behaves, why each replica is checked directly, and that each new key is tested before it goes in the store, while A is tidy but leaves a newcomer to work these points out alone.

author: haiku
reason: A is longer but more complete: it spells out how the transactions and concurrency work (the row lock before the rate-limit count, and the conditional update that lets only one of two submits succeed), has a failure table that covers every step, and points out that the rollback guarantees depend on whether the queue runs in Postgres, while B is easier to skim but leaves the races and failure behavior as open questions or brief notes.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer, but it gives an outsider the whole picture: it defines the basics (sessions, transactions, row locks), handles races A leaves open (it locks the account row for the rate-limit count and uses a conditional update so only one of two submits of a link can save), explains what happens to devices that were logged in, and has a failure table that depends on whether the email queue runs in Postgres, so the system's behaviour is clear without having to guess.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the reasons and knock-on effects a newcomer needs: why only the hash is stored, why the reply is fast and the same on every path, what deleting a session does to a device, and why the rate limit counts every row. Its failure table also puts every failure path in one place; B is tighter and adds a few details (the hidden field, what happens when the breached-password check is down), but it leaves more of the "why" unsaid.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives the reasons behind each choice: why only the token hash is stored, why the API only queues mail, why the rate limit counts rows in every state, and when sessions die relative to the email. It also collects every failure into one table, so a newcomer learns both what happens and why, though A's flow is tighter to scan.
